questions.stem: A neurosurgeon places a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt. Based on the term, this shunt diverts cerebrospinal fluid from the:

options.text: Peritoneal cavity to the bladder
Heart to the lungs
Cerebral ventricles to the peritoneal cavity
Spinal cord to the pleural space

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A ventriculoperitoneal shunt drains CSF from the brain's ventricles into the peritoneal cavity, where it is reabsorbed. Why the others are wrong: **A** it does not connect the peritoneum to the bladder; **B** a heart-to-lung pathway is unrelated to CSF shunting; **D** a spinal-to-pleural shunt is a different (lumbopleural-type) configuration, not a VP shunt.

questions.stem: In CPT, an 'incision and drainage' (I&D) of an abscess is generally distinguished from an 'excision' because an I&D:

options.text: Always removes the entire lesion with margins
Requires a skin graft to close
Is limited to bone procedures
Opens and drains a fluid collection without removing the entire lesion or mass

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An I&D incises and drains a fluid collection (e.g., abscess) but does not excise the whole lesion. Why the others are wrong: **A** removing the entire lesion with margins describes excision; **B** an I&D is typically left to drain or loosely packed, not graft-closed; **C** I&D applies broadly to soft-tissue collections, not just bone.

questions.stem: An interventional radiologist performs a procedure described as 'percutaneous.' In CPT, a percutaneous approach means access is obtained:

options.text: By fully opening the body cavity surgically
Through the skin via needle or small puncture, without an open surgical incision
Through a natural body orifice such as the mouth
Only by laparoscope through the umbilicus

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Percutaneous means access through the skin via a needle or small puncture rather than an open incision. Why the others are wrong: **A** fully opening a cavity is an open approach; **C** access through a natural orifice is a transluminal/endoscopic (e.g., per os) approach; **D** umbilical scope access describes a laparoscopic, not percutaneous, route.

questions.stem: In the male genital subsection, a 'circumcision' code selection often depends on the patient's age and the technique. A key coding distinction is between circumcision performed with a clamp/device versus:

options.text: A diagnostic radiology study
An anesthesia-only service
A pathology consultation
Surgical excision (without a clamp or device)

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** CPT separates circumcision performed using a clamp or other device from circumcision performed by surgical excision, and neonatal versus older patients. Why the others are wrong: **A** a radiology study is unrelated to the surgical technique; **B** anesthesia is a separate service, not the technique distinction; **C** a pathology consult does not define the circumcision method.

questions.stem: A cataract extraction is documented with 'insertion of intraocular lens (IOL) prosthesis' in the same operative session. CPT coding for a routine cataract extraction with concurrent IOL insertion is to report:

options.text: A single combination code that includes both the cataract removal and the IOL insertion
Two separate codes, one for removal and one for the IOL, always with modifier 51
Only the IOL insertion code
An E/M code for the visit instead

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** CPT provides combination codes for cataract extraction with concurrent insertion of an intraocular lens prosthesis, reported as one code. Why the others are wrong: **B** the combined service is one code, not two with modifier 51; **C** reporting only the IOL omits the extraction work; **D** an E/M does not describe the surgical procedure.

questions.stem: Under the current E/M data element scoring, the act of independently reviewing and interpreting an image, tracing, or specimen (that was not separately reported by the same physician) contributes to which MDM element?

options.text: Number and complexity of problems addressed
Risk of complications and morbidity
Amount and complexity of data to be reviewed and analyzed
Total face-to-face time only

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Independent interpretation of a test not separately reported is credited under the data element (amount/complexity of data reviewed and analyzed). Why the others are wrong: **A** the problems element counts the conditions addressed, not data review; **B** the risk element addresses management risk, not interpreting data; **D** time is an alternative selection method, not an MDM data element.

questions.stem: When time is used to select an office/outpatient E/M level under current guidelines, the time counted is:

options.text: The total time personally spent by the physician/QHP on the date of the encounter, including both face-to-face and non-face-to-face work
Only the face-to-face counseling time, and only if counseling dominated the visit
Clinical staff (nurse/MA) time providing the service
Time spent on a different calendar date for the same problem

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Current office/outpatient E/M time is the total physician/QHP time on the encounter date, counting qualifying face-to-face and non-face-to-face activities. Why the others are wrong: **B** the dominant-counseling rule was the legacy standard, not the current total-time rule; **C** clinical staff time does not count toward the physician's time; **D** only time on the date of the encounter is counted.

questions.stem: A pediatrician provides 'critical care' to a critically ill patient. A defining feature of CPT critical care services is that they:

options.text: Are reported only by the surgeon during a global period
Involve high-complexity decision making to treat a critical illness/injury with a high probability of imminent or life-threatening deterioration, and are time-based
Require that the patient be physically located in an emergency department
Are untimed and reported once per admission regardless of duration

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Critical care involves high-complexity decision making for a critically ill/injured patient at high risk of imminent deterioration and is reported using time. Why the others are wrong: **A** it is not limited to a surgeon's global period; **C** critical care can occur in various locations, not only the ED; **D** it is time-based, not a single untimed per-admission charge.

questions.stem: Which two services are typically considered preventive medicine concepts in CPT E/M coding? (Select two.)

options.text: A comprehensive periodic preventive medicine evaluation for an asymptomatic patient (an age-appropriate well visit)
Counseling on risk-factor reduction provided to a well patient
Emergency department evaluation of acute chest pain
Critical care for a patient in septic shock

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Preventive medicine services include age-appropriate comprehensive well visits and risk-factor-reduction counseling for patients without an active illness. Why the others are wrong: **C** evaluating acute chest pain in the ED is problem-oriented, not preventive; **D** critical care for septic shock is acute illness management, not preventive medicine.

questions.stem: In anesthesia coding, when a single anesthesia provider personally administers anesthesia for multiple surgical procedures during the same operative session, the coder generally reports anesthesia for:

options.text: The single procedure with the highest base unit value, plus the total anesthesia time for all the procedures
Every procedure's anesthesia code separately at full value
Only the shortest procedure
The surgeon's primary CPT code with no anesthesia code

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** For multiple procedures under one anesthetic, report the anesthesia code with the highest base value and the combined total anesthesia time. Why the others are wrong: **B** reporting each at full value overstates the single anesthetic episode; **C** the shortest procedure does not drive the base-unit selection; **D** the surgeon's CPT code does not represent the anesthesia service.

questions.stem: A radiology report describes a 'complete' versus a 'limited' abdominal ultrasound. In CPT, a 'complete' ultrasound study generally requires:

options.text: Only that contrast was administered
A minimum of two separate calendar days
Documentation of all required anatomic elements that define that complete study; otherwise the limited code is used
That a surgeon, not a radiologist, performed it

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A 'complete' study requires that every anatomic element defining that exam be evaluated and documented; if not all are imaged, the 'limited' code applies. Why the others are wrong: **A** contrast use does not define complete vs. limited; **B** there is no two-day requirement; **D** the performing specialty does not determine complete vs. limited.

questions.stem: A screening mammography converts to a diagnostic study on the same day because a suspicious finding requires additional views. The HCPCS/CPT modifier used to indicate a screening mammogram converted to a diagnostic mammogram on the same day is:

options.text: Modifier GG
Modifier 26
Modifier 50
Modifier 91

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Modifier GG indicates that a screening mammogram and a diagnostic mammogram were both performed on the same patient, same day, when the screening converts to diagnostic. Why the others are wrong: **B** modifier 26 reports a professional component; **C** modifier 50 reports a bilateral procedure; **D** modifier 91 reports a repeat clinical laboratory test.

questions.stem: In the Pathology and Laboratory section, a Pap smear interpreted using automated 'thin-layer' liquid-based cytology with computer-assisted screening is classified under which subsection of pathology/lab?

options.text: Surgical pathology
Chemistry
Hematology/coagulation
Cytopathology

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Pap smear (cervical/vaginal cytologic) testing falls under cytopathology, which covers cellular specimen examination. Why the others are wrong: **A** surgical pathology covers tissue specimens (gross/microscopic), not cytology smears; **B** chemistry covers analyte testing such as glucose or electrolytes; **C** hematology/coagulation covers blood-cell counts and clotting studies.

questions.stem: A laboratory performs a qualitative drug screen and, on the same specimen, follows with a definitive (quantitative) confirmation of the positive analytes. In CPT drug-testing coding, presumptive and definitive drug testing are:

options.text: Reported with separate code categories—presumptive (screening) testing and definitive (confirmatory) testing are distinct services
Always the same single code
Coded only as an E/M service
Reported only with a radiology code

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** CPT separates presumptive (screening) drug tests from definitive (confirmatory/quantitative) drug tests into distinct code categories. Why the others are wrong: **B** they are not a single combined code; **C** drug testing is a lab service, not E/M; **D** it is laboratory testing, not radiology.

questions.stem: In the Medicine section, psychotherapy 'add-on' codes performed with an E/M service on the same day are reported by:

options.text: Combining all the time into a single E/M code only
Reporting the E/M service and the psychotherapy add-on code together, with psychotherapy time counted separately from the E/M work
Reporting only an anesthesia code
Reporting the psychotherapy as a surgical procedure

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When psychotherapy is provided with an E/M on the same day, the E/M is reported and the psychotherapy add-on code is added, with psychotherapy time tracked separately from E/M activities. Why the others are wrong: **A** the services are distinct and not merged into one E/M; **C** anesthesia coding is unrelated; **D** psychotherapy is a medicine-section service, not a surgical procedure.

questions.stem: In the Medicine section, hemodialysis services for an end-stage renal disease (ESRD) patient managed on an outpatient basis are frequently reported as:

options.text: Monthly capitation-style ESRD-related services based on the number of physician visits and the patient's age
A single surgical global package
Anesthesia base units only
An integumentary destruction code

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Outpatient ESRD-related dialysis management is reported using monthly (capitation-style) codes stratified by the number of physician visits per month and the patient's age. Why the others are wrong: **B** dialysis management is not a surgical global package; **C** it is not valued by anesthesia base units; **D** an integumentary destruction code is unrelated to dialysis.

questions.stem: A cardiologist documents that a diagnostic right heart catheterization and a separately identifiable left heart catheterization were performed. In the Medicine/cardiovascular cath coding family, the foundational principle is that the codes are built around:

options.text: The chambers/sides catheterized and whether congenital anomalies are present, with imaging supervision and injection often bundled into combination codes
The number of staff present in the cath lab
The brand of catheter used
The time of day the procedure started

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Cardiac catheterization coding is organized by which chambers/sides are accessed and whether congenital anomalies are present, with imaging supervision and injections frequently bundled into combination codes. Why the others are wrong: **B** staff count does not drive code selection; **C** catheter brand is irrelevant to the code; **D** start time does not determine the catheterization code.

questions.stem: On a Medicare claim for durable medical equipment, the HCPCS modifiers NU, RR, and UE indicate, respectively:

options.text: New equipment (purchase), rental, and used equipment (purchase)
Left side, right side, and bilateral
Professional, technical, and global components
Initial, subsequent, and sequela encounters

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** For DME, NU denotes new equipment purchased, RR denotes a rental, and UE denotes used equipment purchased. Why the others are wrong: **B** laterality uses LT/RT (and 50 for bilateral); **C** component splits use 26/TC; **D** encounter types are ICD-10-CM seventh characters, not DME modifiers.

questions.stem: A coder needs a code for ambulance transport and certain medical/surgical supplies provided in the office. Which HCPCS Level II alphabetic group primarily contains transportation services and many supplies?

options.text: The J codes
The L codes
The A codes
The V codes

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** HCPCS A codes include transportation (e.g., ambulance) services and many medical/surgical supplies. Why the others are wrong: **A** J codes are drugs administered other than orally; **B** L codes are orthotics and prosthetics; **D** V codes are vision and hearing services/supplies.

questions.stem: Place the steps of correctly assigning a CPT procedure code from an operative note in the proper order, from first to last.

options.text: Identify the main term/procedure performed and look it up in the CPT Index
Note the code or code range the Index points to
Turn to that range in the Tabular and read the section guidelines and any parenthetical notes
Verify the full descriptor matches what was documented and assign the code (with any needed modifier)

questions.explanation: The correct sequence is: locate the procedure as a main term in the CPT Index, note the code or range it cites, turn to that range in the body of CPT to read the applicable section guidelines and parenthetical instructions, and only then verify the full descriptor against the documentation before assigning the code and any modifier. This order matters because the CPT Index merely points to candidates; coding directly from it skips the section guidelines, add-on and 'do not report together' notes, and descriptor details that determine the correct final code.

questions.stem: While abstracting a case, a coder finds the operative note documents a procedure that is more extensive than what the surgeon listed in the header, but the supporting detail is ambiguous. The most compliant next step is to:

options.text: Query the provider for clarification rather than assuming or assigning the higher-level code without support
Assign the most extensive code to maximize reimbursement
Assign the least extensive code regardless of the documentation
Skip coding the procedure entirely

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** When documentation is ambiguous or conflicting, the compliant action is to query the provider for clarification before assigning a code. Why the others are wrong: **B** choosing the higher code to maximize payment without support risks upcoding; **C** defaulting to the lowest code can underreport documented work and is still a guess; **D** omitting a documented procedure is inaccurate coding.

questions.stem: A coder selects the two-digit Place of Service (POS) code '11' on a professional claim. POS code 11 designates which setting?

options.text: Inpatient hospital
Emergency room - hospital
Office
Telehealth provided in the patient's home

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** POS code 11 designates the office setting. Why the others are wrong: **A** inpatient hospital is POS 21; **B** the hospital emergency room is POS 23; **D** telehealth provided in the patient's home is POS 10.

flashcards.back: -ectomy = surgical removal/excision; -ostomy = creation of a new opening; -otomy = cutting into/incision; -plasty = surgical repair/reshaping; -rrhaphy = suturing/repair by suture.

flashcards.front: Directional terms: proximal/distal, medial/lateral, anterior/posterior, superior/inferior
flashcards.back: Proximal = nearer the trunk; distal = farther from it. Medial = toward midline; lateral = away from it. Anterior (ventral) = front; posterior (dorsal) = back. Superior = above; inferior = below.

These notes flag an etiology/manifestation pair. 'Code first' tells you to sequence the underlying cause before the current code; 'Use additional code' tells you to add the manifestation/related code after it.

flashcards.front: ICD-10-CM injury 7th characters A, D, S
flashcards.back: A = initial encounter (active treatment); D = subsequent encounter (routine healing/recovery); S = sequela (a condition arising as a late effect of the injury). The 'X' character is a placeholder, not an encounter value.

Never code straight from the Alphabetic Index. Locate the term in the Index, then verify the code in the Tabular List, applying all instructional notes and required characters before assigning the final code.

Integumentary = 10000 series; musculoskeletal = 20000 series; respiratory/cardiovascular/hemic-lymphatic = 30000 series; digestive = 40000 series; urinary/reproductive/maternity/endocrine = 50000 series; nervous system/eye/auditory = 60000 series.

A surgical code includes the operation, local/topical/digital-block anesthesia, the immediate post-op note, and typical related follow-up care. Unrelated E/M (mod 24/25), staged procedures (58), returns to the OR for complications (78), and unrelated procedures (79) are separately reportable.
Add-on codes describe additional work performed with a primary procedure. They are never reported alone, are exempt from modifier 51 (multiple procedures), and are typically marked with a '+' in CPT.

For office/outpatient visits, the level is chosen by either total time on the date of the encounter OR medical decision making (MDM). History and exam are performed as clinically appropriate but no longer drive the level.

Medical decision making is graded on (1) the number and complexity of problems addressed, (2) the amount and complexity of data reviewed/analyzed, and (3) the risk of complications, morbidity, or mortality of patient management.

P1 = normal healthy patient; P2 = mild systemic disease; P3 = severe systemic disease; P4 = severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life; P5 = moribund, not expected to survive without the operation; P6 = declared brain-dead organ donor.

Modifier 26 reports only the physician's professional work (supervision/interpretation/report). Modifier TC reports only the technical component (equipment, supplies, technologist). Billing the code with no modifier captures the global (both) service.

flashcards.front: HCPCS Level II code letter groups (high-yield)
flashcards.back: J = drugs administered other than orally (injectables/infusions); A = transportation, supplies, administrative; E = durable medical equipment; L = orthotics/prosthetics; G = temporary procedures/services (often Medicare); Q = temporary codes.

flashcards.front: NCCI: edit types and a modifier indicator of 0 vs. 1
flashcards.back: NCCI has PTP (procedure-to-procedure) edits and MUEs (units-of-service limits). A PTP modifier indicator of 0 means the edit can never be bypassed; an indicator of 1 means an appropriate modifier (e.g., 59/X{EPSU}) may bypass it when documentation supports a distinct service.

Covered entities must limit the use, disclosure, and request of protected health information (PHI) to the minimum needed to accomplish the purpose. It does not apply to disclosures for treatment, to the patient, or those the patient authorizes.

Upcoding = reporting a higher-level/more expensive code than documentation supports. Unbundling = billing component services separately instead of the single comprehensive code to increase payment. Both are abusive/fraudulent and can trigger False Claims Act liability.
